blocks.text: **The problem.** Given a binary search tree and two of its nodes `p` and `q`, return their **lowest common ancestor** — the deepest node that has both `p` and `q` in its subtree. A node counts as its own ancestor.

blocks.alt: The tree with root 6. For p = 3 and q = 5: both are below 6, so go left to 2; both are above 2, so go right to 4; 3 is below 4 and 5 is above it, so they split here and 4 is the answer.

p = 3, q = 5  ->  4

blocks.text: In a general binary tree you'd have to search both subtrees. In a BST the values tell you where p and q are. If **both** are smaller than the current node, both live in the left subtree — so does their LCA. If both are bigger, go right. The first node where they **split** (one on each side, or one of them is the node) is the answer.
1. Ignore the order: general binary-tree LCA
The classic binary-tree solution works on a BST too: ask each subtree whether it contains p or q, and the node where both sides answer "yes" is the LCA.
**Time O(n), space O(h).** It may visit every node — it never uses the ordering.
**Time O(h), space O(h)** for the call stack — one call per level on a single path.
3. The same walk as a loop

blocks.caption: Both smaller: go left. Both bigger: go right. Otherwise this node is where they split.

blocks.alt: General binary-tree LCA: O(n) time, O(h) space. Recursion on values: O(h) time, O(h) space. Loop on values: O(h) time, O(1) space.

items: **p is an ancestor of q** — the answer is p itself.
**p = q** — the answer is that node.
**p and q on opposite sides of the root** — the root.
**A skewed tree** — h = n, so O(h) becomes O(n).
**LCA of a binary tree** — no ordering to follow; approach 1 is the answer there.
**Distance between two nodes in a BST** — depth(p) + depth(q) − 2·depth(LCA).
**LCA where p or q may be missing** — search for both first, then run the walk.
